reference.source: American Academy of Sleep Medicine ICSD-3
clinicalPearls: A non-REM parasomnia in which the person is partially awakened from deep sleep and appears confused and disoriented in time and place
Behaviour is typically slow and clumsy rather than the fearful, agitated flight of a sleep terror
Episodes arise from slow-wave sleep, usually in the first third of the night, and there is amnesia for the event
It is most common in young children and tends to diminish with age
Priming factors include sleep deprivation, other sleep disorders such as apnoea, shift work and certain sedatives
Management centres on reassurance, adequate sleep and treating any underlying sleep disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Confusional arousals reflect incomplete transition out of slow-wave sleep, so that arousal systems partially activate while the brain remains largely in deep sleep, producing a mixed state of wakefulness and sleep. This dissociation, favoured by factors that deepen sleep or fragment it, leaves cognition and orientation impaired during the episode. As with other non-REM parasomnias there is a genetic predisposition and a tendency to run in families, and precipitants that increase slow-wave sleep pressure or cause arousals trigger events.
additionalDifferentials: Nocturnal hypoglycaemia or other metabolic causes of confusion
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from a characteristic history and event description
Screening for precipitants such as sleep deprivation and obstructive sleep apnoea
Video polysomnography if events are atypical, injurious or possibly epileptic
redFlags: Injurious or aggressive behaviour during episodes
New onset in an adult without clear precipitant
Associated excessive daytime sleepiness suggesting untreated apnoea
reference.prognosis: The disorder is benign and usually self-limiting, particularly in children, with events reduced by adequate sleep and by addressing precipitating factors.
pitfalls: Confusing confusional arousals with sleep terrors or nocturnal seizures
Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea as a driver in adults
Attributing an adult's new confusional episodes to parasomnia without excluding metabolic or epileptic causes
Failing to address sleep deprivation as a key precipitant
references: American Academy of Sleep Medicine ICSD-3
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine
management: Reassure the person and family that events are benign and typically self-limiting, especially in children, and educate carers on gentle guidance back to sleep without forced waking
Optimise sleep hygiene with adequate, regular sleep to reduce slow-wave sleep pressure and sleep fragmentation
Identify and treat coexisting sleep disorders that provoke arousals, particularly obstructive sleep apnoea
Review and where possible withdraw precipitating sedatives and mitigate shift-work-related sleep disruption
Institute bedroom safety measures to prevent injury during episodes
Consider scheduled pre-emptive awakenings for stereotyped recurrent events, reserving a benzodiazepine only for frequent or injurious episodes refractory to behavioural measures
Refer to sleep medicine for video polysomnography if events are atypical, injurious or possibly epileptic
